evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Fujitsu and New Mexico announced a collaboration to establish a quantum computing research center focused on hardware, software, algorithms, theory and workforce development.

The collaboration will examine hybrid systems combining Fujitsu’s FUJITSU-MONAKA processors with quantum computing, quantum simulation and AI for potential applications in materials, energy, drug discovery and other industries.

Left to right: Senator Michael Padilla, Cabinet Secretary New Mexico Economic Development Rob Black, Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, Fujitsu CTO Vivek Mahajan and Senator George Muñoz (Provided) PRESS RELEASE — Fujitsu announced a collaboration with New Mexico to establish a quantum computing research center in New Mexico.

The center will conduct advanced research spanning quantum computing hardware, software, algorithms, and theory, while supporting education and workforce-development initiatives designed to expand the quantum talent pipeline and strengthen collaboration across industry, academia, government, and the research community.
The initiative will bring together Fujitsu’s expertise in advanced computing and quantum technologies with New Mexico’s scientific and research ecosystem.

Through research collaboration, internships, academic engagement, and other workforce-development programs, the center will help create new pathways for students, researchers, and engineers to participate in the emerging quantum economy.

The collaboration also supports the State of New Mexico’s broader vision of building a more interconnected, innovative, and sustainable future through investments in advanced technologies and high-skilled industries.
New Mexico has emerged as an important center for quantum research and technology development.
The State has committed US$150 million to support investments alongside companies seeking to establish or expand quantum computing operations and develop the broader quantum ecosystem in New Mexico.
Fujitsu and the State of New Mexico will explore opportunities to participate in and support these initiatives.

As part of the collaboration, Fujitsu and the State will explore opportunities for joint research that leverage New Mexico’s concentration of scientific and academic institutions, including Sandia National Laboratories, Los Alamos National Laboratory, the University of New Mexico, and New Mexico State University.
Fujitsu and New Mexico State University (NMSU) already collaborate on research and development activities related to the FUJITSU-MONAKA CPU and associated high-performance computing solutions.

items.originalTitle: This robotic arm could change how drones launch in combat
items.summary: Sesame Solar, Target Arm and AG3 Labs have launched what they describe as the first Made-in-USA Persistent Drone Operations Nanogrid. The integrated system combines mobile power generation, autonomous drone launch and recovery, and configurable small drones into one package for forward and expeditionary operations. evidenceRecords.text: Sesame Solar, Target Arm and AG3 Labs have launched what they describe as the first Made-in-USA Persistent Drone Operations Nanogrid.
The integrated system combines mobile power generation, autonomous drone launch and recovery, and configurable small drones into one package for forward and expeditionary operations.
The idea is relatively straightforward: instead of sending personnel out to launch, recover, charge, and redeploy individual drones, the Nanogrid is designed to automate much of that cycle.
At the center of the system is Sesame Solar’s Mobile Power Hub, which uses solar power, hydrogen, and battery storage to generate and store electricity for equipment in the field.
The company says its solid-state, low-pressure hydrogen can be transported by land, sea, or air, eliminating the need for conventional fuel resupply.
The US Army has previously highlighted the lack of standardized procedures for getting backup power to drone teams in the field.
The three companies say their system is intended to address that gap while reducing the need for personnel to remain exposed during drone operations.
Target Arm provides the robotic side of the equation with its Ralar autonomous launch and recovery system.
The robotic arm can deploy and recover drones, while integrated drone magazines allow multiple aircraft to be cycled through missions, charging, and storage.
Ralar is also designed to operate from moving vehicles and boats.
That means a team does not necessarily have to stop its vehicle just to launch or recover a drone.
AG3 Labs supplies the aircraft through its SPADE platform, a Group 1 small unmanned aircraft system designed to be reconfigured for different missions.
The platform can also be operated individually or as part of an autonomous swarm, potentially allowing a single operator to manage multiple aircraft.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Stickney Crater Explanation: Stickney Crater, the largest crater on the martian moon Phobos, is named for Chloe Angeline Stickney Hall, mathematician and wife of astronomer Asaph Hall.
Asaph Hall discovered both the Red Planet’s moons in 1877.
Over 9 kilometers across, Stickney is nearly half the diameter of Phobos itself, so large that the impact that blasted out the crater likely came close to shattering the tiny moon.

This enhanced-color image of Stickney and surroundings was recorded by the HiRISE camera onboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter as it passed within some six thousand kilometers of Phobos in March of 2008.
Even though the surface gravity of asteroid-like Phobos is less than 1/1000th Earth’s gravity, streaks suggest loose material slid down inside the crater walls over time.
The origin of the curious grooves along the surface is mysterious but may be related to tidal stresses experienced by close-orbiting Phobos or the crater-forming impact itself.

items.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
items.originalTitle: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
items.summary: This post is about improving the impact of our scheduling decisions. We recently replaced a priority-based scheduler with a system including GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract. As a result, we shifted the debate about how much GPU time each research project deserves from a case-by-case operational task to a transparent administrative budgeting process. At Ai2, we manage thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs arranged in clusters ranging in size from 88 to 1024 GPUs.

evidenceRecords.text: This post is about improving the impact of our scheduling decisions.
We recently replaced a priority-based scheduler with a system including GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract.
As a result, we shifted the debate about how much GPU time each research project deserves from a case-by-case operational task to a transparent administrative budgeting process.
At Ai2, we manage thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs arranged in clusters ranging in size from 88 to 1024 GPUs.

These clusters are built for large-scale distributed training of AI models, and they serve a group of about 150 internal researchers whose work covers a diverse set of AI domains, including the full model flow of LLM and VLM training, robotics reinforcement learning (RL) simulation, and post-training for scientific agentic use cases.
Like many labs, we have demand for GPU time that far exceeds supply.
Based on submitted workloads, at any moment in time we have outstanding requests for 2-3x more GPUs than are available.
One way to think about this is that every available GPU hour on our cluster has 2-3 different research workloads competing for it.
Historically, we used a priority-based scheduler, and we allowed workloads to opt out of preemptability.

Citing documents shared with OpenAI's financial backers, the FT said the company put its annualized revenue at close to $50 billion as of the end of September. evidenceRecords.text: OpenAI is bringing in about $20 billion less in annualized revenue than investors had been led to believe, the Financial Times reported Thursday, raising questions about the solidity of the AI business.

Media reports late last month had pegged the figure at $70 billion based on information given to investors.

Investors track annualized revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic as the clearest signal of demand for artificial intelligence, and the figures help justify enormous spending on data centers as well as the AI-fueled stock market rally.

In an apparent pushback, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the earlier number, which the network reported as $68 billion, counted gross revenue from OpenAI's partnerships with companies like chipmaker Nvidia.
That method was intended to make it easier for investors to measure the company against chief rival Anthropic.
The report weighed on AI-linked stocks, with Nvidia down 2.9%, SpaceX down 4% and Oracle losing nearly 6%.

items.originalTitle: Earth from Space: Namibia’s biggest salt pan
items.summary: The image was acquired at the beginning of the dry season, when average daily temperatures typically range from 14°C to 30°C. Water is also still present in the smaller salt pans that dot the landscape northwest of the Etosha Pan, the biggest of which is the Natukanaoka Pan. evidenceRecords.text: The image was acquired at the beginning of the dry season, when average daily temperatures typically range from 14°C to 30°C.
Water is also still present in the smaller salt pans that dot the landscape northwest of the Etosha Pan, the biggest of which is the Natukanaoka Pan.
The water in these small ‘lakes’ appears in shades of green and blue.
The Ekuma river, near the centre of the image, is seen flowing from Lake Oponono at an elevation of about 1200 m above sea level, southwards to the salt flat at 1030 m.
Lake Oponono is able to hold water from one wet season to the next and is a habitat for flamingos and cattle.
The vegetation surrounding the Etosha Pan – shown in striking red by Sentinel-2’s near-infrared channel – consists mainly of grassland, savannas and mopane woodland.
Mopane trees are the dominant type of vegetation across the eastern and central areas of the national park, showing up as dark, vibrant red in this image.
They provide a habitat for elephants, giraffe and leopards.
The savannahs, in the west and southern areas of the park, are home to wildebeest, lions and springbok.
Patches of red are also visible on the Etosha Pan, suggesting vegetation is present.
While few plants thrive in the salty clay terrain, some types of blue-green algae and salt-tolerant grasses have adapted to the harsh environment.
Sentinel-2 carries a multispectral imager, which detects light in 13 spectral bands – in contrast to the human eye, which can see only three spectral bands (red, blue and green).

items.title: NASA Announces Bold Science Initiatives for America’s Golden Age Summit
items.originalTitle: NASA Announces Bold Science Initiatives for America’s Golden Age Summit
items.summary: NASA is launching two new science and technology initiatives to deepen scientific understanding and accelerate the innovation that will shape America’s future in space. The initiatives are announced in conjunction with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy’s (OSTP) “Science: A Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday with top U.S. agency leaders. The programs reflect NASA’s commitment to pioneering research and transformative technologies and advancing the Trump Administration’s vision as outlined in the July report to the President, Science: A New Golden Age.

evidenceRecords.text: NASA is launching two new science and technology initiatives to deepen scientific understanding and accelerate the innovation that will shape America’s future in space.

The initiatives are announced in conjunction with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy’s (OSTP) “Science: A Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday with top U.S. agency leaders.

The programs reflect NASA’s commitment to pioneering research and transformative technologies and advancing the Trump Administration’s vision as outlined in the July report to the President, Science: A New Golden Age.
“NASA has a proud history of pursuing bold ideas and achieving the near impossible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, we are building on that legacy by creating new opportunities for great science, experimenting with how we evaluate and accelerate the best ideas, and investing in the next generation of researchers through the Genesis Mission Fellowships.

We are entering a new Golden Age of American innovation and discovery, and NASA will be at the forefront.” During a fireside chat, Isaacman and Michael Kratsios, assistant to the President for science and technology and director of OSTP, will discuss the following: Establishing a coordinated metascience initiative within NASA’s Science Mission Directorate to strengthen the reliability, efficiency, transparency, and overall productivity of the agency’s scientific practices.
As part of this effort, NASA is expanding the agency’s use of dual anonymous peer review to ensure proposals are evaluated solely on their intrinsic scientific merit.
Started as a pilot program during the first Trump Administration, this initiative has helped position NASA as a leader in advancing best practices in scientific review.
NASA will support 10 Genesis Mission Fellows, who are accelerated doctoral students with dual competencies in super intelligence (SI) and science or engineering.
Fellows will work directly on NASA mission areas and conduct research at NASA laboratories, advancing SI-enabled scientific discovery.
The fellowships will be based on NASA’s successful Future Investigators in NASA Earth and Space Science and Technology program.
Through these new initiatives, NASA will continue to inspire the world and drive progress in science and technology.
